sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Delphi
sites.summary: Rome consulted Delphi as early as the tradition of Tarquin's sons, and in 216 BC sent Fabius Pictor after Cannae. Sulla plundered its treasures in 86 BC. Plutarch, priest here c. 95-125, wrote on why the oracle now spoke in prose and had only one Pythia where once there were three. The Pythian games and oracle lingered into the 4th century; the 'last oracle' to Julian's physician Oribasius is probably a later Christian invention. Theodosian legislation of 391-392 closed it.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia
sites.summary: The games went on under Rome: Sulla moved the 175th Olympiad (80 BC) to Rome, and Nero competed in 67 in a special postponed festival, winning the chariot race despite falling out. The last attested victor is the Armenian boxer Varazdates (385). The traditional end of the games under Theodosius I in 393 is late and uncertain; a fire under Theodosius II (c. 426) is reported. Phidias' Zeus was taken to Constantinople, where it burned in the Lauseion fire of 475.

sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Didyma
sites.summary: The colossal unfinished Hellenistic temple near Miletus. Caligula wanted to finish it for his own cult. In 303 Diocletian consulted the oracle, which replied that 'the just on earth' prevented true prophecy, a response that Constantine later remembered as the trigger of the Great Persecution. Julian made himself prophet of the shrine; Christian chapels were later built inside.

sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Claros
sites.summary: Colophon's oracle, at its height in the 2nd century AD. The prophet drank from a sacred spring in an underground chamber beneath the temple; Tacitus tells of Germanicus' visit in AD 18 and the prediction of his early death. Inscriptions record delegations from cities as far as Britain and Dalmatia seeking verse oracles against the Antonine plague.
scholarship: Parke, The Oracles of Apollo in Asia Minor (1985)

sites.name: Sanctuary of Demeter at Eleusis
sites.summary: Home of the Mysteries, into which Romans eagerly sought initiation: Sulla, Cicero, Augustus (31 BC), Hadrian (124/5 and again as epoptes), Lucius Verus, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus (176). Marcus rebuilt the sanctuary after the Costoboci raid of 170. Valentinian I's ban on night rituals in 364 was waived for Eleusis by the proconsul Praetextatus. Eunapius says Alaric's Goths, guided by Christian monks, sacked it in 396.

sites.name: Oracle of Ammon at Siwa
sites.summary: The desert oracle that greeted Alexander as son of Zeus. By Strabo's day it was almost abandoned, he says, because the Romans preferred the Sibylline books and Etruscan haruspicy. Pausanias saw Pindar's hymn inscribed there. Siwa's Christianisation is obscure.

sites.name: Heliopolis (Baalbek) sanctuary
sites.summary: The largest temple complex of the Roman world, built over 150 years on a colony of Augustus: the Temple of Jupiter Heliopolitanus (begun late 1st century BC, finished under Nero), with 20 m columns resting on a podium including the Trilithon blocks of c. 800 tonnes, and the 2nd-century 'Temple of Bacchus'. Macrobius says Trajan tested the oracle by sending sealed blank tablets. Theodosius built a basilica in the great court.

sites.name: Artemision of Ephesus
sites.summary: One of the Seven Wonders, rebuilt after Herostratus' arson of 356 BC. Its right of asylum was confirmed by Caesar and Augustus, who limited its extent. Paul's preaching provoked the silversmiths' riot ('Great is Artemis of the Ephesians'). Goths sacked it c. 262. The temple was quarried in late antiquity; tradition, probably false, has its columns reused in Hagia Sophia.

sites.name: Pessinus, sanctuary of the Great Mother
sites.summary: Phrygian temple-state of Cybele and her galli. In 204 BC, following a Sibylline oracle, Rome obtained from Attalus I the goddess's black aniconic stone and brought it to the Palatine, received by Scipio Nasica as 'best man in Rome' and Claudia Quinta. Julian visited in 362 and wrote his hymn to the Mother of the Gods.

sites.name: Comana Pontica (Ma-Enyo)
sites.summary: Temple-state of the goddess Ma, with, Strabo says, over 6,000 temple servants and a priest second only to the king. Strabo's maternal kinsman Dorylaus held the priesthood under Mithridates VI; Pompey gave it to Archelaus, Caesar to Lycomedes. A festival city frequented by merchants and prostitutes, which Strabo compares to Corinth.

sites.name: Comana in Cappadocia
sites.summary: Original seat of Ma-Enyo, whose cult Sulla brought to Rome as Bellona. Strabo says the priest held power second to the king and the temple owned over 6,000 servants of both sexes.

sites.name: Temple of Atargatis at Hierapolis Bambyce
sites.summary: Temple of the Syrian Goddess described by Lucian (or his imitator) in De Dea Syria: eunuch galli who castrated themselves in ecstasy, sacred fish in the lake, and two phallic towers climbed twice a year. Crassus plundered the treasury in 54 BC before Carrhae.

sites.name: Temple of Elagabal at Emesa
sites.summary: Shrine of the sun god Elagabal, worshipped as a black conical stone, whose hereditary priests were the family of Julia Domna. The boy priest Varius Avitus became emperor in 218 and took the stone to Rome. Aurelian credited the god with his victory at Emesa over Zenobia in 272.

sites.name: Doliche (Jupiter Dolichenus)
sites.summary: Hilltop sanctuary of the Commagenian Baal on Dülük Baba Tepesi, origin of a cult spread by soldiers to the Rhine, Danube and Hadrian's Wall. Excavations since 2001 confirmed the temple, destroyed when Shapur I took Doliche c. 253, after which the cult faded in the West too.

sites.name: Temple of Jerusalem
sites.summary: The Second Temple, rebuilt from 520-515 BC. Pompey entered the Holy of Holies in 63 BC; Crassus robbed it in 54. Herod rebuilt it from 20/19 BC on a platform of 14 ha. Josephus says over a million died in the siege of 70, when Titus' troops burned the Temple on 9-10 Ab. Its menorah appears on the Arch of Titus, and the fiscus Iudaicus diverted the Temple tax to Jupiter Capitolinus. Julian's rebuilding attempt failed in 363.

sites.name: Temple of Onias at Leontopolis
sites.summary: Jewish temple founded c. 160 BC by the priest Onias IV in the nome of Heliopolis (Tell el-Yahudiya), with Ptolemaic consent. After the fall of Jerusalem, Vespasian ordered it closed in 73, fearing it would become a new focus of revolt.

sites.name: Mount Gerizim
sites.summary: Holy mountain of the Samaritans. Their temple was destroyed by John Hyrcanus c. 111/110 BC; Hadrian built a temple of Zeus Hypsistos. In 484, after a Samaritan revolt, Zeno built a church of the Theotokos on the summit; the great revolt of 529 under Justinian ended in massacre.

sites.name: Temple of Isis at Philae
sites.summary: The last functioning temple of the old Egyptian religion. A treaty of Diocletian allowed the Blemmyes and Nobades to worship here; the last hieroglyphic inscription is dated 24 August 394 and the last demotic graffito to 452. Procopius says Justinian ordered Narses to close it c. 535-537, imprison the priests and send the cult statues to Constantinople.

sites.name: Serapeum of Alexandria
sites.summary: Ptolemaic temple of Sarapis on its acropolis, holding Bryaxis' great statue and the 'daughter library'. In 391, after riots, Theophilus' Christians with imperial backing demolished it and smashed the statue: Rufinus describes the axe-blow and the mice running from the head. Its fall was a defining moment for both pagans and Christians.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis
sites.summary: Latin federal sanctuary on Lake Nemi, served by the rex Nemorensis, a runaway slave who won the office by killing his predecessor (the starting point of Frazer's Golden Bough). Caligula's two great ships were moored on the lake; recovered in 1929-32, they burned in 1944.

sites.name: Jupiter Latiaris on Mons Albanus
sites.summary: Summit of Monte Cavo, site of the Feriae Latinae, at which the consuls had to preside before leaving for their provinces. Generals refused a triumph in Rome could celebrate one here (first by Papirius Maso in 231 BC). The paved Via Sacra to the summit survives.

sites.name: Fanum Voltumnae
sites.summary: Federal sanctuary of the Twelve Etruscan Peoples near Volsinii, where they met in council and debated aid to Veii (Livy). Excavations at Campo della Fiera, Orvieto, since 2000 are the best candidate. Constantine's Hispellum rescript (333-337) allowed the Umbrians to hold their festival at home instead of at Volsinii.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia
sites.summary: Terraced sanctuary of the late 2nd century BC climbing the hillside of Praeneste, where oracular lots (sortes) carved on oak were drawn by a boy. Its Nile mosaic is the finest Hellenistic floor in Italy. Cicero mocks the lots; Tiberius tried and failed to suppress them, and Domitian consulted the goddess every year.

sites.name: Lavinium (Penates and Thirteen Altars)
sites.summary: Ritual centre of the Latins, where Rome's consuls and dictators sacrificed to the Penates and Vesta on entering office. The Thirteen Altars and the heroon claimed as Aeneas' tomb were excavated from 1955.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Epidaurus
sites.summary: Healing sanctuary of Asclepius. In 292 BC, during a plague, a Roman embassy brought back a sacred snake, which swam ashore on the Tiber Island where Asclepius' temple was built. Inscribed cure tablets record dream healings.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Pergamon
sites.summary: Rebuilt in the 2nd century with a round temple modelled on the Pantheon. Aelius Aristides spent years here as an incubant and recorded his dreams in the Sacred Tales; Galen trained here and treated gladiators. Caracalla visited for treatment in 214.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Cos
sites.summary: Terraced healing sanctuary near the home of the Hippocratic school. Claudius' doctor Gaius Stertinius Xenophon, a Coan (who Tacitus says helped poison him), got the island tax immunity in 53.

sites.name: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace
sites.summary: Mystery sanctuary of the Cabiri, whose initiation protected sailors. Perseus of Macedon fled here after Pydna in 168 BC and was captured. Romans traced their Penates to Samothrace; Germanicus tried to visit for initiation in AD 18 but was turned back by contrary winds.

sites.name: Oracle of Zeus at Dodona
sites.summary: The oldest Greek oracle, consulted by inscribed lead tablets. Sacked by Aetolians in 219 BC and devastated with the rest of Epirus in 167, when Aemilius Paullus enslaved 150,000 Epirotes; restored under Augustus.

sites.name: Temple of Aphrodite at Aphrodisias
sites.summary: City privileged by Octavian, who wrote that he had chosen it from all Asia; the archive wall preserves his letters. The temple of Aphrodite was converted into a church c. 500 by moving its columns outward, and the city was renamed Stauropolis.

sites.name: Plutonium of Hierapolis
sites.summary: Cave gate of Hades emitting lethal carbon dioxide. Strabo tested it with sparrows that died instantly, while castrated galli could enter unharmed; Dio says he tried it too. Rediscovered in 2013 with the temple, theatre seats and pool.

sites.name: Temple of Athena Ilias
sites.summary: Rome's claimed mother-city. Ilium got tax privileges after 190 BC and from Caesar, a supposed descendant of Aeneas. Fimbria sacked it in 85 BC, boasting he had taken in 11 days what Agamemnon needed 10 years for. Julian visited in 354 and found a bishop tending the pagan shrines.

sites.name: Oracle of Glycon at Abonuteichos
sites.summary: Alexander of Abonuteichos created the oracle of Glycon, a human-headed snake (a puppet, says Lucian), in the 150s. Its fame reached Rome: Marcus Aurelius followed its advice to throw two lions into the Danube, and the senator Rutilianus married Alexander's daughter. Coins of the town show Glycon into the 3rd century.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Aphrodite at Paphos
sites.summary: Aphrodite's birthplace sanctuary, worshipped as a conical stone. Titus visited in 69 on his way to Judaea and consulted the priest about his future; Tacitus describes the cult and the rule that no blood touched the altar.

sites.name: Temple of Bel, Palmyra
sites.summary: Dedicated on 6 April AD 32, the great temple of Palmyra's chief god combining Greek columns with a Near Eastern cella. Aurelian's troops looted it in 273 and he paid for its repair. Converted to a church, later a mosque; blown up by ISIS in 2015.

sites.name: Temple of the Moon at Carrhae (Harran)
sites.summary: Ancient centre of the moon god Sin. Caracalla was murdered on 8 April 217 riding from Edessa to the moon temple at Carrhae; Julian sacrificed there in 363. Harran stayed pagan beyond the end of Roman rule, its 'Sabians' surviving into the 11th century.

sites.name: Temple of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme
sites.summary: Mountain-top temple of Mercury Dumias of the Arverni. Pliny says the Greek sculptor Zenodorus spent ten years and 40 million sesterces making a colossal bronze Mercury for the Arverni before Nero summoned him to make the Colossus.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Apollo Grannus at Grand
sites.summary: Healing sanctuary in the Vosges, probably the 'most beautiful temple in the world' where, according to the panegyric of 310, Constantine saw Apollo and Victory offering him laurel wreaths promising 30 years of rule: the pagan precursor of his Christian vision of 312. Its astrological diptych of ivory survives.

sites.name: Fontes Sequanae (source of the Seine)
sites.summary: Healing spring of the goddess Sequana with a temple and portico. Over 200 wooden ex-votos of body parts and pilgrims, preserved in the mud, and a bronze of the goddess in a duck-shaped boat were excavated in 1963.

sites.name: Temple of Sulis Minerva, Bath
sites.summary: Temple and spa over the hot spring, built in the Flavian period. The sacred spring yielded 130 curse tablets asking the goddess to punish thieves of cloaks, rings and money, and around 12,000 coins.
scholarship: Tomlin, in Cunliffe (ed.), The Temple of Sulis Minerva at Bath II (1988)

sites.name: Temple of Nodens, Lydney Park
sites.summary: Late Roman healing sanctuary above the Severn with temple, guest-house, baths and long abaton for incubation, excavated by Mortimer and Tessa Wheeler in 1928-29, with J.R.R. Tolkien contributing a note on the name Nodens. A curse tablet asks Nodens to recover a stolen ring.

sites.name: Nehalennia sanctuaries (Domburg and Colijnsplaat)
sites.summary: Coastal temples of the goddess Nehalennia at the Scheldt mouth. Over 240 altars, dredged from the sea since 1970, were set up by traders in wine, salt, fish sauce and pottery crossing to Britain, thanking her for safe passage.

sites.name: Tophet of Carthage (Salammbô)
sites.summary: Precinct of Baal Hammon and Tanit with thousands of urns of infant and animal cremations under stelae. Whether they were child sacrifices, as Greek and Roman writers and the Hebrew Bible claim, or a cemetery for infants, is a long debate; recent analysis favours sacrifice. Saturn's cult continued the tradition under Rome.
sites.debate: Sacrifice (Stager, Xella et al. 2013) versus infant cemetery (Schwartz et al. 2010).

sites.name: Temple of Caelestis at Carthage
sites.summary: Temple of Juno Caelestis, Romanised Tanit, the chief goddess of African Carthage. Elagabalus brought her statue to Rome to marry Elagabal. Bishop Aurelius turned it into a church c. 399, and Quodvultdeus says it was razed in 421.

sites.name: Hispellum rescript
sites.summary: Constantine's rescript allowed the Umbrians to build a temple to the gens Flavia at Hispellum and hold their festival there, on condition that it was not polluted by 'the deceits of contagious superstition', meaning sacrifice. Imperial cult survived Christianisation as a civic honour.

sites.name: Temple of Augustus at Tarraco
sites.summary: In AD 15 Tiberius allowed the Spaniards to build a temple to Augustus at Tarraco, 'setting an example for all provinces'. Quintilian preserves Augustus' joke when told a palm had sprouted on his altar there: 'that shows how often you light it'. The provincial cult complex covered the upper town.

sites.name: Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum
sites.summary: Provincial cult centre of the Three Gauls at the confluence of Rhône and Saône, inaugurated by Drusus on 1 August 12 BC (or 10 BC). Each year delegates of the 60 Gallic civitates met in the concilium Galliarum and elected a priest. Its amphitheatre was the site of the martyrdom of Blandina and companions in 177.

sites.name: Ara Ubiorum (Cologne)
sites.summary: Altar of Rome and Augustus for Germania, founded as the counterpart of Lugdunum when the province was meant to reach the Elbe. In AD 9 its priest, the Cheruscan Segimundus, tore off his fillets and joined Arminius.

sites.name: Temple of Roma and Augustus at Pergamon
sites.summary: In 29 BC Octavian allowed the koinon of Asia to build him a temple at Pergamon (with Roma), and Bithynia one at Nicomedia, the first provincial imperial cult temples, for provincials only; Romans were to worship Roma and Divus Julius at Ephesus and Nicaea. The temple has not been securely located.

sites.name: Temple of Roma and Augustus at Nicomedia
sites.summary: Bithynia's provincial imperial cult temple, authorised together with Pergamon in 29 BC. Pliny the Younger, governing Bithynia c. 110, conducted the loyalty sacrifices that Christians refused, prompting his famous letter to Trajan.

sites.name: Temple of Augustus and Roma at Ancyra
sites.summary: Temple of the provincial cult of Galatia whose walls carry the best copy of Augustus' Res Gestae in Latin and Greek, discovered by Busbecq's party in 1555 and published by Mommsen. Later a church.

sites.name: Temple of Divus Claudius, Camulodunum
sites.summary: Temple of the deified Claudius in the veteran colony, built at the Britons' cost and seen as 'a citadel of eternal domination'. Boudica's rebels besieged the last defenders in it for two days in 60. Its podium vaults survive under Colchester Castle.

sites.name: Temple of Tiberius, Livia and the Senate at Smyrna
sites.summary: In AD 26 eleven cities of Asia competed before the Senate for the right to build a temple to Tiberius, Livia and the Senate; Smyrna won over Sardis by citing its ancient loyalty, including a temple to Roma in 195 BC.

sites.name: Temple of the Sebastoi, Ephesus
sites.summary: Ephesus' first provincial neokorate temple, dedicated in 89/90 to the Flavian emperors; a colossal head and forearm of Titus (or Domitian) survive. Neokoros ('temple warden') titles became prizes in the rivalry of Asian cities.

sites.name: Altar of the Numen of Augustus at Narbo
sites.summary: The plebs of Narbo vowed an altar to the numen of Augustus in AD 11; the inscription sets out the dates of annual sacrifices, including Augustus' birthday, and the rules modelled on the altar of Diana on the Aventine.

sites.name: Mithraea of Ostia
sites.summary: Ostia has around 18 known mithraea, the densest cluster anywhere. The Mithraeum of the Seven Spheres and the Mithraeum of Felicissimus, whose floor mosaic shows the symbols of the seven grades of initiation (Raven to Father), are key evidence for the cult's structure.
scholarship: Becatti, Scavi di Ostia II: I mitrei (1954)

sites.name: Mithraeum under San Clemente
sites.summary: Late 2nd-century mithraeum in a courtyard of a Roman house, beneath the 4th-century basilica of San Clemente. It preserves the cult relief of Mithras killing the bull and benches for the meal, overlaid by the Christian church in one of Rome's most vivid stratigraphies.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Santa Prisca
sites.summary: Aventine mithraeum with painted processions of the grades and verse inscriptions, one possibly dated by consuls to 202. The paintings were damaged in antiquity, perhaps by Christians.
scholarship: Vermaseren & van Essen, The Excavations in the Mithraeum of the Church of Santa Prisca (1965)

sites.name: Mithraeum at Carrawburgh (Brocolitia)
sites.summary: Small mithraeum outside the fort on Hadrian's Wall, with three altars dedicated by prefects of the First Cohort of Batavians. It was desecrated in the early 4th century, perhaps by Christians. The nearby well of Coventina yielded over 13,000 coins.

sites.name: London Mithraeum (Walbrook)
sites.summary: Mithraeum built c. 240 beside the Walbrook stream, found in 1954, when 30,000 people queued to see it. Its marble heads of Mithras, Serapis and Minerva were buried in the 4th century. Rebuilt on its original site beneath the Bloomberg building in 2017.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: Founded c. 168 by Palmyrene archers of the Roman garrison and enlarged c. 240, with paintings of Mithras as a mounted hunter and of two Magi-like figures. Moved to Yale. With the synagogue and church it shows three religions within metres of each other.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Capua
sites.summary: Underground mithraeum with the best surviving fresco of the tauroctony and scenes of initiation (blindfolded initiates kneeling before a mystagogue).

sites.name: Carnuntum: the altar of 308
sites.summary: Carnuntum had several mithraea. At the conference of November 308, Diocletian, Galerius and Licinius restored a mithraeum and dedicated an altar to the Unconquered Sun Mithras, 'protector of their rule'.

sites.name: Mithraea of Poetovio
sites.summary: Five mithraea at the customs station of Poetovio, the first run by customs slaves of the portorium Illyricum, the third by soldiers of legions V Macedonica and XIII Gemina in Gallienus' reign.

sites.name: Mithraea of Nida (Heddernheim)
sites.summary: Civil settlement north of Frankfurt with at least four mithraea, one with a double-sided rotating relief, evidence of the cult's popularity in the Rhine provinces.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Huarte (Hawarte)
sites.summary: Mithraeum near Apamea with 4th-century paintings of Mithras fighting demons, found in 2000 beneath a church built over it, probably c. 400, a direct case of Christian supersession.

sites.name: Synagogue of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: House synagogue rebuilt in 244/245 with walls covered in biblical paintings (Moses, Exodus, Ezekiel's valley of bones), overturning the idea that Judaism banned figural art. It was buried in the rampart built against the Sasanian siege of 256, which preserved it. Now in Damascus.

sites.name: Synagogue of Sardis
sites.summary: The largest ancient synagogue known, a converted hall of the bath-gymnasium complex, 80 m long, with over 80 donor inscriptions, many by city councillors. It shows a wealthy, integrated Jewish community until the city's destruction in 616.

sites.name: Synagogue of Ostia
sites.summary: Found in 1961 near the ancient shore, the oldest synagogue building in Europe, with a 1st-century phase and a 4th-century Torah shrine; an inscription honours Mindius Faustus for the ark. Jews of Ostia served the port trade.

sites.name: Synagogue of Capernaum
sites.summary: Limestone synagogue of the 4th-5th century over a basalt 1st-century building, perhaps the synagogue where the Gospels place Jesus' teaching. Opposite it a church was built over the 'house of Peter'.

sites.name: Synagogue of Delos
sites.summary: Building near the shore identified as a synagogue of the 2nd-1st century BC, among the oldest in the diaspora; an inscription of Samaritans of Delos was found nearby.

sites.name: Synagogue of Gamla
sites.summary: One of the earliest synagogue buildings in the land of Israel, destroyed when Vespasian stormed Gamla in 67 after a siege; Josephus says 4,000 died and 5,000 threw themselves from the cliffs.

sites.name: Hammath Tiberias and the rabbinic academies
sites.summary: Synagogue with a 4th-century mosaic of the zodiac around Helios in his chariot. Tiberias was the seat of the Jewish patriarchate and the academy where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled c. 400.

sites.name: Synagogue of Beth Alpha
sites.summary: 6th-century synagogue mosaic signed by Marianos and his son Hanina, with the binding of Isaac, a zodiac and a Torah shrine, found by kibbutzniks in 1928.

sites.name: Sepphoris
sites.summary: Galilean city where Judah ha-Nasi completed the Mishnah c. 200. A 5th-century synagogue mosaic has a zodiac and the binding of Isaac; the 'Mona Lisa of Galilee' Dionysian mosaic shows a pagan elite alongside.

sites.name: Synagogue of Stobi
sites.summary: Inscription of Claudius Tiberius Polycharmus, 'father of the synagogue', who gave the ground floor of his house for the synagogue while keeping the upper floor for his family.

sites.name: Synagogue of Naro (Hammam Lif)
sites.summary: Synagogue near Carthage whose mosaic, found in 1883, has a Latin dedication by Juliana 'for her salvation', menorahs and marine scenes; part is in the Brooklyn Museum.

sites.name: Great Synagogue (Diplostoon) of Alexandria
sites.summary: Rabbinic sources describe a vast double-colonnaded synagogue where officials signalled the responses with flags. Philo records the attacks on the Alexandrian synagogues in 38. It was destroyed in the Diaspora revolt of 115-117.

sites.name: Christian house of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: The earliest securely identified church building: a house adapted c. 232 with a baptistery painted with the Good Shepherd, Adam and Eve, the healing of the paralytic, Christ walking on water and the women at the tomb. Buried in 256.

sites.name: Prayer hall of Kefar Othnay (Megiddo)
sites.summary: Christian prayer hall in a Roman army camp, found in 2005, with a mosaic of c. 230 naming 'the God Jesus Christ' and the donor Akeptous, and a centurion Gaianus who paid for the floor.

sites.name: Theodorian basilica of Aquileia
sites.summary: Twin halls built by Bishop Theodore (who signed at Arles in 314) with the largest early Christian floor mosaic in the West: Jonah, the Good Shepherd, donors' portraits and marine scenes, preserved beneath the medieval cathedral.

sites.name: Double cathedral of Trier
sites.summary: Twin basilicas built from c. 330 over a palace whose painted ceiling, perhaps showing Fausta or Helena, was smashed and buried. The core of the present cathedral is a 4th-century square hall.

sites.name: Lullingstone villa house-church
sites.summary: Upper room of a Kentish villa painted c. 350-370 with chi-rho monograms and praying figures (orantes), the earliest Christian wall painting in Britain.

sites.name: Hinton St Mary mosaic
sites.summary: 4th-century villa mosaic in Dorset with a bust of a man before a chi-rho, probably the earliest portrait of Christ in Britain, beside Bellerophon killing the Chimaera.

sites.name: Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
sites.summary: Built under Constantine c. 333 over the cave of the Nativity, with an octagon above the grotto; rebuilt under Justinian after the Samaritan revolt of 529. Jerome and Paula founded monasteries here in 386, where Jerome made the Vulgate.

sites.name: San Vitale, Ravenna
sites.summary: Octagonal church begun under Bishop Ecclesius and funded by the banker Julianus Argentarius, consecrated in 547 by Maximian. Its apse mosaics of Justinian and Theodora with their courts are the defining images of the reconquest.

sites.name: Sant'Apollinare in Classe
sites.summary: Basilica consecrated in 549, also funded by Julianus Argentarius, with an apse mosaic of St Apollinaris amid sheep and a jewelled cross in a starry sky.

sites.name: Etchmiadzin cathedral
sites.summary: Mother church of Armenia at Vagharshapat, by tradition founded by Gregory the Illuminator after Tiridates III's conversion (c. 301 or 314), rebuilt in 483/484. Armenia's adoption of Christianity probably preceded Constantine's.

sites.name: Svetitskhoveli, Mtskheta
sites.summary: Royal church of Iberia (eastern Georgia), traditionally founded after King Mirian's conversion by the captive woman Nino c. 330s, a story Rufinus heard from the Iberian prince Bacurius.
